issues.legal_issue: The state legislature is competent to impose a tax on land holdings, including agricultural land.
material_facts: The enactment imposed a tax on land holdings, with the tax measured by reference to their annual value.
The holdings covered by the enactment included agricultural land.
issues.conclusion: The enactment was within the state legislature’s competence because the constitutional power to tax land includes agricultural land.
issues.legal_principle: Constitutional entries conferring legislative power are given a liberal construction, and broad terms extend to matters reasonably included within them. The Court relied on Navinchandra Mafatlal, Bombay v. Commissioner of Income-tax, [1955] 1 SCR 829, and United Provinces v. Mt. Atiqa Begum, [1940] FCR 110. The separate entry for taxes on agricultural income did not exclude agricultural land from the entry concerning taxes on land.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_holding: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a tax imposed on land holdings.
predicates.tax_is_imposed_on_land_holdings: The enactment imposes a tax on land holdings, even if it uses the land’s value to measure the tax.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a tax imposed on land holdings, the state legislature has competence to impose that tax.

issues.legal_issue: A law allowing the executive to select a valuation multiple up to a prescribed ceiling does not require different multiples for every district or class of land, and a notification applying permitted variations complies with that law.
material_facts: The enactment set a maximum multiple for determining annual value and permitted different multiples for districts, areas, or classes of land.
The State Government prescribed a multiple within the ceiling and used different multiples for certain categories of land and areas.
The Court considered local conditions and differences in land quality relevant to setting the multiples.
issues.conclusion: The word permitting different multiples conferred discretion rather than imposing a duty to prescribe different multiples in every instance. The notification complied with the statutory requirements.
issues.legal_principle: The word “may” is construed in its context; here it did not mean “shall” or “must.” The legislature set a maximum and left the executive discretion to adjust the multiple to local conditions and the qualities of land. The Court applied section 5(1) of the U.P. Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957.

predicates.land_value_is_calculated_using_a_multipl: The annual value of land is determined by multiplying a rent-based amount by a selected multiple.
predicates.law_sets_a_maximum_multiple_and_allows_v: The governing law sets a ceiling for the multiple and permits variation by area or land category.
predicates.government_sets_multiples_within_the_cei: The government selects multiples within the ceiling and varies them for relevant areas or kinds of land.

issues.definition: If land value is calculated using a multiple, the law caps that multiple while permitting relevant variation, and the government stays within the cap and makes relevant variations, its valuation notification complies with the law.

issues.legal_issue: A taxing statute is open to challenge under fundamental-rights guarantees, but a levy based on land value and a guided valuation discretion do not, on the facts considered, violate equality or the right to hold property.
material_facts: The enactment taxed holdings above a specified size and based the tax on annual value determined from rent and a multiple.
The tax rates increased by graduated bands tied to annual value.
The law limited the government’s choice of multiple and contemplated adjustment to local conditions and land quality.
The assessment scheme provided for notice, an opportunity to be heard, appeal, and revision.
The petitioner challenged the valuation discretion and tax rates as unequal and as an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold property.
issues.conclusion: A tax law can be challenged under Part III of the Constitution, but the challenges to the valuation discretion and the rates under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) failed. The discretion was not unfettered, and the tax’s basis and graduated rates did not establish a violation.
issues.legal_principle: A taxing statute is subject to fundamental-rights review. The Court relied on Mohammad Yasin v. Town Area Committee, Jalalabad, [1952] SCR 578; State of Bombay v. United Motors (India) Ltd., [1953] SCR 1069; Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. v. State of Bihar, [1955] 2 SCR 603; Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh, [1956] SCR 393; and Balaji v. Income-tax Officer, [1962] 2 SCR 983. Under Article 14, a tax may be invalid if it imposes an obviously unequal burden on the same class of similarly situated property; rational classifications and different rates for different classes are permissible. A tax law may also be examined under Article 19(1)(f), particularly where it leaves assessment and recovery machinery entirely to executive choice. Here, the tax’s basis, the legislature’s general policy, the bounded discretion, and the assessment procedure defeated the challenges.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law and tax_applies_to_a_defined_class_of_large_holdings and tax_is_based_on_annual_land_value and rates_are_gradated_by_value and valuation_discretion_is_guided_by_general_policy and assessment_provides_notice_hearing_and_review

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law: A party challenges a tax law as infringing constitutional rights.
predicates.tax_applies_to_a_defined_class_of_large_: The tax applies to holdings within a defined class based on their size.
predicates.tax_is_based_on_annual_land_value: The amount of tax is determined by reference to the annual value of the land.
predicates.rates_are_gradated_by_value: The applicable tax rate changes across graduated bands of annual value.
predicates.valuation_discretion_is_guided_by_genera: The executive’s valuation choices are bounded by a statutory ceiling and guided by stated considerations such as local conditions or land quality.
predicates.assessment_provides_notice_hearing_and_r: The assessment process provides notice, an opportunity to be heard, and routes for appeal or revision.

issues.definition: A tax scheme of the described kind does not violate equality or the right to hold property when it taxes a defined class by annual land value, uses graduated rates, guides valuation discretion, and provides procedural safeguards.

issues.legal_issue: A valid tax law does not violate the constitutional protection against deprivation of property merely because the tax is burdensome; a tax is not an acquisition or requisition of property.
material_facts: The challenged enactment imposed a tax and did not purport to acquire or requisition the petitioner’s property.
The petitioner invoked Article 31 against the tax.
The Court found no violation of other fundamental rights that would make the law invalid.
issues.conclusion: The challenge under Article 31 failed: Article 31(2) did not apply to the tax, and a tax imposed under an otherwise valid law satisfied Article 31(1).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(1) requires deprivation of property to be authorized by a valid law. Article 31(2) concerns acquisition or requisition and does not apply to a taxing statute, even if an excessive tax might ultimately cause loss of property. The Court also relied on Articles 31(2A) and 31(5)(b)(i), which support that distinction.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_law: A party challenges a tax law under constitutional property protections.
predicates.levy_is_a_tax_not_an_acquisition_or_requ: The law requires payment of a tax and does not purport to acquire or requisition property.
predicates.law_is_otherwise_valid: The tax law does not otherwise infringe a fundamental right or exceed legislative competence.

issues.definition: A tax imposed by an otherwise valid law does not violate the property guarantee when the law taxes rather than acquires or requisitions property.

issues.legal_issue: A taxing enactment is not colourable merely because its tax is alleged to be excessive; the challenge requires evidence supporting an inference that taxation is a device to confiscate property.
material_facts: The petitioner alleged that cultivation costs left little net income and that the tax was confiscatory.
The respondents disputed those calculations and supplied figures indicating that the petitioner’s net income substantially exceeded the tax assessed.
The petitioner did not provide information about the rent used to determine annual value, an important basis for assessing the burden.
The Court found that the statutory scheme did not disclose a constitutional infirmity in its charging or assessment provisions.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner did not establish that the enactment was confiscatory or a colourable exercise of legislative power, and the challenge failed.
issues.legal_principle: Excessiveness of a tax alone does not establish colourable legislation; relevant circumstances must justify an inference of fraud on legislative power. The Court considered K. T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, [1961] 3 SCR 77, but explained that it involved discriminatory and unreasonable provisions as well as a confiscatory effect, and did not authorize courts to strike down a tax simply because its rate was high.

predicates.colourable_legislation_challenge_to_tax: A party alleges that a tax law is a pretence for an exercise of legislative power aimed at confiscating property.
predicates.tax_burden_alone_is_not_supported_by_rel: The claim that the tax consumes the taxpayer’s property or income is not established by reliable evidence.
predicates.no_other_circumstances_show_a_confiscato: The evidence does not otherwise indicate a design to use taxation as a device for confiscating property.

issues.definition: A colourable-legislation challenge fails when an alleged excessive tax burden is not reliably shown to be confiscatory and no other circumstances establish a confiscatory design.
